strengths: Introduces a simple, well-motivated, and theoretically grounded metric (VIG) that decomposes cleanly into a KL-divergence interpretation and token-level loss differences, giving both sample- and token-level granularity.

Extensive empirical validation of VIG as a diagnostic tool: qualitative examples with controlled image swaps (Tab. 1), benchmark-level distribution analysis aligning with known modality dependency (Fig. 2), and POS-tag/token-level analysis (Fig. 3, 4, Tab. 2) that convincingly show VIG highlights visually salient words (colors, nouns, attributes) versus function words.

Strong and broad empirical results: VIG-guided selective training improves performance while using substantially fewer active tokens (34-79% reduction) across four different model/architecture combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V, Open-Qwen2VL), suggesting reasonably good generalization.
Thorough comparison against multiple existing debiasing baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), showing VIG training is competitive and orthogonal/complementary to these methods (combined gains).

Good set of ablations: selection-level ablation (sample-only vs sample+token), selection-ratio sweep, text-only benchmark preservation check, and data-distribution/long-tail analysis, which collectively support the core claims and address several natural robustness questions.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility appendix (hyperparameters, thresholds per model, compute environment, dataset details).
weaknesses: The core VIG computation depends on an ad hoc heuristic (Gaussian-blurred images) to simulate 'absence of vision,' borrowed from another paper; there is no analysis of sensitivity to blur strength or alternative no-image conditions (e.g., black image, no image token at all), which could materially affect the ranking/thresholds and downstream selection.

The method reuses a single threshold τp for both sample- and token-level selection purely to avoid extra hyperparameters, but no ablation isolates whether this joint design is actually optimal versus tuning sample and token thresholds separately; this design choice is asserted rather than justified empirically.

VIG is computed using models 'after the pre-training stage' only, and it is unclear how robust the metric/selection is to using a different or partially-trained backbone for scoring (e.g., using a stronger LLM backbone might change perplexity gaps substantially, especially since PPL-based measures can be sensitive to model calibration).

Statistical significance is not reported anywhere (single-run numbers throughout Tables 3, 4, 6, F.1, F.3); given some gains are modest (e.g., MMBench +0.87, POPE F1 +0.03), it's hard to assess whether improvements are consistently above noise, especially given LVLM instruction-tuning is known to have run-to-run variance.

The paper claims VIG-guided training 'mitigates language bias fundamentally at the representational level' but the causal mechanism is only supported by correlational analyses (attention fraction, corruption robustness); no ablation directly isolates whether gains stem from reduced language bias per se versus simply from improved data quality/curation (similar to standard data-pruning benefits unrelated to modality bias).

Baseline comparisons in Sec 4.3 are conducted only on LLaVA-1.5 7B; it remains unclear whether the competitive/complementary advantage over VCD/PAI/VAR/LACING generalizes to larger models or other architectures tested elsewhere in the paper.

The computational overhead of VIG scoring (additional forward passes per training sample) is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantified relative to the savings in training compute from token/sample pruning, making it hard to judge net efficiency gains in practice.

Some hyperparameter differences across baselines in Table 4 (e.g., LACING's own training-based tuning) may not be perfectly comparable to VIG training's setup, and the paper does not discuss whether baselines were retrained/optimized under identical compute budgets.

strengths: The core metric, Visual Information Gain (VIG), is simple, well-motivated, and grounded in a clean theoretical derivation connecting it to cross-entropy loss and KL divergence, giving a principled interpretation as the reduction in prediction divergence from providing the image.

The empirical validation of VIG as an indicator of visual grounding is thorough: sample-level VIG aligns with known benchmark-level modality dependencies (COCO/POPE vs. GQA/SQA), and token-level VIG cleanly separates visually grounded content words (colors, poses) from function words (articles, prepositions), which is intuitive and convincing.

The selective training scheme is tested across three different model/scale combinations (LLaVA-1.5 7B, 13B, ShareGPT4V 7B) and consistently improves performance while using substantially fewer tokens (e.g., 12.14M vs 58.61M for the 13B model), demonstrating good data efficiency.

Comparisons against multiple existing bias-mitigation baselines (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING) show that VIG training is competitive or superior without architectural changes or inference overhead, and is shown to be complementary/orthogonal to these methods when combined.

Mechanistic analyses (attention allocation to visual tokens across layers, and robustness to textual corruption/'blind faith in text') provide converging evidence that the method changes model behavior in the intended direction, not just aggregate benchmark numbers.
Ablations on selection level (sample-only vs. sample+token) and selection ratio p are included, supporting the necessity of both components and giving some sense of sensitivity to the hyperparameter.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: thresholds, hyperparameters, training time, and qualitative examples are reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: The 'no-image' condition used to compute VIG relies on Gaussian-blurred images (following prior work), which may retain low-frequency visual cues (color palette, coarse scene layout); this could bias VIG scores in ways not analyzed, and no alternative ablation-free image removal (e.g., black/masked image, text-only forward pass) is compared to test sensitivity of the metric to this design choice.

Several evaluation benchmarks used are quite small (LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild has 60 questions, MM-Vet 218 questions) and are scored by LLM judges (GPT-4/GPT-3.5) known to have run-to-run variance; the paper reports single-run point estimates with no error bars, standard deviations, or multiple seeds, making it hard to assess whether the often small reported gains (e.g., +0.03 POPE F1, +0.20 DocVQA accuracy) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The threshold τ_p is reused for both sample- and token-level selection to avoid extra hyperparameters, but the derived τ_70 values differ substantially and even in sign across models (-0.021, 0.046, -0.042), and there is no ablation decoupling sample- and token-level thresholds to show that this coupling is actually optimal rather than just convenient.

The paper does not compare VIG-based selection against simpler perplexity/loss-based data selection baselines that do not require a separate 'without-image' forward pass (e.g., selecting samples/tokens by absolute loss, by length, or by difficulty), so it is unclear how much of the benefit comes specifically from the visual contrast versus generic difficulty-based curriculum/data pruning effects.

All experiments are conducted on the LLaVA-1.5/ShareGPT4V architecture family sharing similar backbones (Vicuna + CLIP), despite the related work section referencing more modern architectures (Qwen2-VL, InternVL); generalization to different vision encoders, connector designs, or larger/more recent LVLMs is not empirically tested, limiting the evidence for broad applicability.

The claim that VIG training 'improves visual grounding' rests substantially on proxy signals (attention-to-image ratio, corrupted-text robustness) rather than more direct grounding tests (e.g., localization, referring expression accuracy), leaving some ambiguity about whether the underlying mechanism is genuinely enhanced visual reliance or simply reduced overfitting to generic textual patterns in the (now smaller, filtered) answer distribution.

The computational overhead discussion is somewhat understated; while framed as a 'one-time cost,' VIG computation requires additional forward passes with both blurred and real images over the entire training set using the aligned model, and no wall-clock/FLOP comparison against baseline data-selection costs is given to substantiate practicality at larger scale.
